title: Mass on a spring

reference.basis: no known-size object visible in the plane of motion

slow_motion.evidence: no caption, narration or visual indication of slow motion; motion appears as a real-time animation

subjects.description: small green rectangular block attached to the bottom end of the vertical spring

observation.what_happens: A small green block hanging from a vertical spring oscillates up and down above a black-and-white striped bar. It is already in motion at the start of the clip and continues oscillating without being touched or stopping through the end.

calibration.note: scale from the fall itself: 1 px/s² over 1 arc = g of 9.807 m/s²

given: g = 9.807 m/s² (Earth); it set the scale, so treat g as known and fixed
reasoning: Path is a straight vertical line with s~y, period ~0.58 s, peaks shrinking and troughs rising, so a vertical spring oscillator with weak damping in air. Candidates go from ideal SHM to linear viscous, to linear+quadratic aero drag, to nonlinear spring, all using s and fixed g.

caveats: Natural rest length lies far outside the seen travel, so it is only weakly pinned down.
Mean residuals tip from low early to high mid-clip, but the wobble stays small.
Quadratic drag and cubic stiffness were already tried and did not help.
critique.finding: The block bobs up and down on its spring around {s_nat} and slowly loses energy to air drag {gamma}.
critique.headline: Spring block bobs on, gently slowed by air.
critique.why_it_won: It fades just right with plain air drag, while adding quadratic drag only makes the future wobble worse.

headline: Spring block bobs on, gently slowed by air.
finding: The block bobs up and down on its spring around 741 m and slowly loses energy to air drag 0.35 ± 8.49e-4 1/s.

eyeball.confidence: low - only a single static frame was visible so period, scale and decay cannot be measured; values are plausible typical lab spring-mass guesses
eyeball.law_in_words: Vertical mass on linear spring with viscous damping, s measured downward from support: s_double_dot = g - w0^2*(s - s_nat) - gamma*s_dot, where w0^2=k/m is stiffness per mass acting on stretch from unstretched position s_nat, g is gravity, and gamma is viscous damping per mass.
